screeningScope: Full-text source, eligibility, study-design, taxonomy, and synthesis-readiness review of queue positions 1-12 after Batch 06 publication.

decisionDefinitions.INCLUDE: Eligible for evidence extraction and synthesis after full-text review.
decisionDefinitions.DEGRADED: A required source or verification element was unavailable.

records.sourceFile: Strength and power thresholds to identify high and low linear sprint speed performers in collegiate American football players.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: A cross-sectional classification analysis of 294 NCAA football players divided into high- and low-body-mass groups tested whether relative strength and power measures distinguished faster from slower 40-yard-dash performers. Receiver-operating-characteristic areas ranged from 0.695 to 0.903, with vertical jump and broad jump providing the strongest discrimination in both body-mass groups and relative hang clean and squat adding group-specific information.
records.limitations: The analysis used a median speed split, hand-timed 40-yard dashes, jump-mat measures, and 3-repetition-maximum lifts. Nutrition and hydration were not controlled, the sample was limited to male collegiate football players, and the proposed thresholds were not prospectively or externally validated.
records.synthesisCaution: Use the reported cut points as sample-specific classification references, not causal training prescriptions or universal standards. Thresholds differ by body-mass group, testing method, and roster context.

records.sourceFile: The Effects of Sleep Extension on the Athletic Performance of Collegiate Basketball Players.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Eleven Stanford men's basketball players completed a 2- to 4-week habitual-sleep baseline followed by 5 to 7 weeks of sleep extension with a goal of at least 10 hours in bed. Objective sleep increased by about 111 minutes; sprint time improved from 16.2 to 15.5 seconds, free-throw accuracy by 9 percentage points, three-point accuracy by 9.2 percentage points, and vigilance, sleepiness, and mood measures also improved.
records.limitations: This was a small, single-team, uncontrolled pre-post study without randomization, crossover, or a concurrent comparison group. Season timing, practice exposure, accumulated sleep debt, and expectancy may have contributed to the changes, and the sample included only healthy male collegiate basketball players.
records.synthesisCaution: The findings support identifying and correcting insufficient sleep, but they do not prove that a 10-hour time-in-bed target independently caused every performance improvement or that the same dose is required for every athlete.

records.sourceFile: Elite North American soccer performance in thermally challenging environments  - An explorative approach to tracking outcomes.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Match observations from 37 elite male soccer players across four North American seasons linked GPS outcomes and differential ratings of perceived exertion with kickoff temperature, weekly temperature change, and heat index. Thermal variables had trivial-to-small relationships with total distance; higher temperature and heat index were associated with small reductions in high-speed running, and heat index had a small positive relationship with breathlessness RPE.
records.limitations: The observational sample was unbalanced because players contributed between 3 and 98 matches. Wet-bulb globe temperature was unavailable, and fixture congestion, substitutions, hydration, cooling strategies, travel, tactics, and acclimatization could not be fully controlled.
records.synthesisCaution: Treat ambient conditions as one contextual layer in match monitoring. The small associations do not justify deterministic heat-based workload reductions or universal thresholds without athlete-level response and environmental context.

records.sourceFile: Evaluating the relationship between neurological function, neuromuscular fatigue, and subjective performance measures in professional rugby union players.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Eleven senior professional rugby union players completed neurological, heart-rate-variability, reactive-strength, mood, and injury-status testing three times weekly during a six-week midseason period. Reactive strength index modified had only a weak negative correlation with direct-current potential, while the different objective and subjective measures generally provided nonredundant information.
records.limitations: This short case series involved 11 male players from one professional setting, no control group, and a proprietary neurological-readiness system whose underlying algorithm was not independently evaluated. Repeated observations do not overcome the limited athlete count or establish long-term predictive validity.
records.synthesisCaution: Use neurological, neuromuscular, autonomic, and subjective data as complementary signals. The weak associations do not validate any single measure or proprietary score as a stand-alone readiness or injury-risk decision rule.

records.sourceFile: The Sprint Mechanics Assessment Score - A qualitative screening tool for the in-field assessment of sprint running mechanics.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: The 12-item Sprint Mechanics Assessment Score was applied to maximum 35-m sprint video from 136 elite soccer players, with 36 players used for reliability analysis. Intrarater reliability was good at ICC 0.828 and interrater reliability was good at ICC 0.799, both with a 1-point standard error of measurement; item-level agreement ranged from 75.0% to 88.8% within raters and 66.6% to 88.8% between raters.
records.limitations: The study evaluated scoring reliability, not prospective injury prediction, responsiveness to coaching, or performance improvement. Reliability was based on one sprint trial and assessors familiar with the method; transfer to novice raters, other sports, developmental levels, and symptomatic athletes remains uncertain.
records.synthesisCaution: Use the score to structure shared observation and flag mechanics for deeper assessment. Reliability alone does not establish that a higher score predicts injury or that changing an item will improve performance or reduce risk.

records.sourceFile: Validating InBody 570 multi-frequency bioelectrical   impedance analyzer vs DXA for body fat percentage analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: In 110 recreationally active university adults aged 18 to 25 years, InBody 570 multifrequency bioelectrical impedance estimates correlated strongly with DXA body-fat percentage at r = 0.94. However, InBody produced a lower mean body-fat estimate than DXA, 20.99% versus 25.61%, and the overall and subgroup differences were statistically significant.
records.limitations: Strong correlation does not demonstrate agreement or interchangeability, and the report did not present a Bland-Altman analysis. The young university sample, self-reported preparation compliance, unverified hydration status, and device-specific algorithm limit generalization.
records.synthesisCaution: Use the same device and standardized preparation for longitudinal monitoring, and interpret change against device-specific error. Do not substitute InBody and DXA values or treat their absolute body-fat percentages as equivalent.

records.sourceFile: Adverse Effects of Anabolic Androgenic Steroid Abuse in Athletes and Physically Active Individuals - A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This systematic review and meta-analysis associated anabolic-androgenic steroid abuse with higher systolic blood pressure by 12.43 mmHg, diastolic pressure by 8.09 mmHg, LDL cholesterol by 9.12 mg/dL, AST by 14.47 U/L, and ALT by 12.16 U/L, along with testosterone lower by 141.57 ng/dL. The pooled findings support multisystem cardiovascular, hepatic, and endocrine concern.
records.limitations: Included studies varied in quality, exposure type, dose, duration, and outcome measurement and were vulnerable to selection, publication, polysubstance, and comorbidity bias. Much of the exposure evidence was observational, so pooled differences should not be treated as precise causal effects for an individual athlete.
records.synthesisCaution: Use the review to support confidential screening, education, and medically supervised evaluation, not to infer use from a single biomarker. Suspected use and withdrawal require individualized clinical assessment.

records.sourceFile: Association of Lower Limb Compression Garments During HighIntensity Exercise with Performance and Physiological Responses- A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Across 23 randomized controlled trials in athletes and physically active adults, lower-limb compression garments worn during high-intensity exercise did not materially improve running performance, vertical jump, maximal or submaximal oxygen uptake, blood lactate, or perceived exertion. For example, the pooled 50- to 400-m running difference was 0.06 seconds and the RPE difference was -0.20 units, both with confidence intervals spanning no effect.
records.limitations: Randomization and allocation procedures were incompletely reported in several trials, and the performance synthesis was dominated by running tasks with heterogeneous garment pressures and protocols. Shared control groups and pooled distances complicate some comparisons, and the review addressed use during exercise rather than all postexercise recovery outcomes.
records.synthesisCaution: Do not expect lower-limb compression garments worn during intense exercise to create a reliable acute performance advantage. Athlete comfort or recovery preferences should be evaluated separately from performance claims.

records.sourceFile: Athlete Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators Abuse - A Systematic Review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This systematic review included 72 articles on athlete selective androgen receptor modulator use, performance-related effects, and adverse outcomes. Available surveys estimated use at roughly 1% to 3%; 13 case reports described 15 mostly young adult men, and the broader clinical, preclinical, and product literature raised hepatic, cardiovascular, endocrine, tendon, and supplement-contamination concerns.
records.limitations: The evidence mixed surveys, trials, animal studies, product analyses, and case reports without meta-analysis. Only four SARMs were emphasized, case reports cannot establish incidence or attribution, co-supplementation was common, abstracts were excluded, and athlete prevalence data were limited.
records.synthesisCaution: No SARM is approved for athlete performance use. Ask directly and nonjudgmentally about supplements and SARMs, verify products and symptoms, and involve appropriate medical and anti-doping resources rather than assuming claimed product contents or safety.

records.sourceFile: Biomechanical Determinants of Change of Direction Performance - A Systematic Review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Thirteen studies involving 374 participants examined biomechanical correlates of preplanned 45- to 180-degree change-of-direction performance. Faster performances were generally associated with shorter ground-contact times, greater approach and exit velocities, larger braking and propulsive forces, greater trunk inclination, a lower center of mass, and task-specific joint moments and power.
records.limitations: The evidence was correlational, 79.4% of participants were male, and tasks varied substantially by angle, approach speed, technique, and timing method. Reactive or unplanned change of direction was not studied, and evidence for sex-specific, training-status, or sport-specific moderators was sparse.
records.synthesisCaution: Match assessment and coaching to the task angle and athlete strategy. The identified correlates are not universal causal cues, and optimizing one biomechanical feature may trade off against another or against joint loading.

records.sourceFile: Blood flow-restricted training for  lower extremity muscle weakness due to knee pathology - A systematic  review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Nine controlled studies, including eight level-1 studies, compared blood-flow-restricted exercise with conventional rehabilitation in 165 patients and 170 controls with ACL reconstruction, knee arthroscopy, osteoarthritis, or patellofemoral pain. Six of seven strength studies reported significant benefits, while evidence for muscle cross-sectional area and hamstring outcomes was more limited; no training complications were reported.
records.limitations: Samples were small and protocols differed in cuff type, pressure, load, duration, and knee condition. Most outcomes emphasized quadriceps strength, statistical significance was not consistently tied to clinically meaningful change, and the absence of reported complications in these studies does not establish broad safety.
records.synthesisCaution: Blood-flow-restricted training is a supervised load-management option when heavy loading is not tolerated, not a default replacement for progressive resistance exercise. Screen contraindications and individualize cuff pressure, dose, and progression.

records.sourceFile: Can caffeine change the game - Effects of acute caffeine intake on specific performance in intermittent sports during competition - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Twenty-four double-blind randomized crossover studies involving 399 participants assessed acute caffeine during competition or competition-like intermittent sport. Doses of approximately 3 to 6.4 mg/kg increased the number of sprints, impacts, accelerations, decelerations, offensive efforts, and successful sport-specific actions, with small-to-moderate standardized mean differences.
records.limitations: Sports, caffeine forms, timing, doses, and performance outcomes were heterogeneous, and only two studies assessed blinding. Expectancy, habitual caffeine use, adverse effects, sex-specific responses, and late-day sleep costs were inconsistently evaluated; the evidence reflects acute response rather than chronic benefit.
records.synthesisCaution: Trial caffeine individually in training before competition, use the lowest effective dose, and weigh any acute benefit against anxiety, gastrointestinal effects, cardiovascular symptoms, and sleep disruption. Team-average effects do not guarantee an athlete-level response.
